title: Record-breaking California tides cause major flooding of roads and businesses
summary:
Beaches close as Los Angeles and La Jolla see all-time high tides and big waves batter landmark pier in Pacifica

Super El Niño weather brought record-breaking high tides up and down the…

blocks.text: Super El Niño weather brought record-breaking high tides up and down the California coast on Wednesday, sending seawater rushing into beachside communities and flooding roads and businesses.

As big waves battered the coast, the tip of a landmark pier in Pacifica, south of San Francisco, was slammed into the sea, local news outlets reported. The pier, which had once housed a favorite local cafe, had previously suffered structural damage and had been closed to the public, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.

Los Angeles and Santa Barbara tied or broke all-time high tide records on Wednesday, at 8.19 and 8.21ft, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). La Jolla, California, just north of San Diego, also set an all-time high tide record of 8.11ft (2.5 meters), according to the National Weather Service, while preliminary data suggested that tides in Monterey, south of San Francisco, might also have set an all-time record at 8.03ft.
The city of Monterey closed multiple beaches to the public over safety concerns, with closures lasting until Friday.
“That sun may be out, but the beach and surf zone remain dangerous,” NWS San Francisco warned, citing waves around the San Francisco Bay area as high as 24ft.

blocks.caption: Waves crash while a king tide and a series of storms begin to hit the Pacific north-west in Pacifica, California. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters

blocks.text: In Pacifica, local video and live streams showed giant crashing waves, tide waters sweeping over beaches and piers, and flooded coastal roads. Tide waters flooded areas of including Highway 1, including near the famous local landmark Taco Bell Cantina, America’s poshest Taco Bell, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.
Low-lying coastal roads around the Bay Area saw flooding, including a stretch of road near the Golden Gate Bridge, which was temporarily closed, the Chronicle reported.
Wednesday’s blue skies and early reports suggested that most of the state is on track to avoid the worst-case scenario – coastal flooding amplified by intense winter rainstorms.

“We’re past high tide, and San Francisco has made it through the worst of this round of king tides,” mayor Daniel Lurie said in a social media statement just after noon local time, saying officials were “only aware of minimal impacts across the city”.

Local officials had been preparing for weeks for the risk that flooding would disrupt travel during Thanksgiving week, one of the busiest times of the year. Experts warn that flooding risk will only worsen in the next two months.

Flooding risk at San Francisco international airport, a major transit hub situated on low-lying coastal land, had been of particular concern. At least three airlines offered free trip changes to travelers whose journeys took them through San Francisco on Wednesday, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.
But the airport announced at noon that “We’re in the clear,” and said it was deactivating its emergency operations center after avoiding any impact from the high tides on Tuesday and Wednesday.

On the north coast, the National Weather Service reported that Humboldt Bay saw its second highest tide on record, and advised residents to prepare for major coastal flooding in low lying areas. The county sheriff warned the public to stay away from beaches during the storm.

A local news outlet in Oregon shared a video on Tuesday that illustrated the risk of the west coast’s high-tide surf, showing a man and his dog almost getting swept away by unexpectedly high waves during the king tides in Cannon Beach, Oregon. Both man and dog escaped without injury, police told KVAL News.

blocks.caption: A  flooded neighborhood during a king tide event in Pacifica, California. Photograph: Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Citing Wednesday’s forecast, some cities on California’s central coast, including Santa Cruz, Monterey and Carmel-by-the-Sea, announced they would be closing beaches starting on Tuesday evening because of the potential dangers, KSBW Action News reported.

“California took early action to prepare for El Niño, and we’re continuing that work by strengthening flood defenses, positioning emergency supplies, and coordinating with local emergency crews to reduce risks to communities,” California governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement on Tuesday, warning residents to take extra caution when preparing for holiday travel.

The California governor’s office of emergency services deployed crews and equipment around the state to assist with storm response. In the Bay Area, crews could be seen preparing sandbags to help protect buildings from flooding.

California’s flooding risk this week is the result of a combination of factors, some of them driven by this year’s super El Niño weather, including the lingering effects of the massive Kelvin wave that traveled up California’s coast. The overlap of unusually high Pacific coast water levels this year with the seasonal high tides called “king tides” has sparked alarm from weather experts, who have warned that the most dangerous flooding is likely to occur if a strong winter storm with heavy wind and rain hits areas of the coast at the same time as the high tide’s peak.

So far, it seems like California has avoided the worst of that risk during the November king tide period. But the amplified king tides will return twice more, around late December and then in late January, in periods where big winter storms remain likely.
Dani Anguiano contributed reporting
